label: The thesis
blurb: The reading nobody assigned and the chapter that will not come. The degree lives or dies here.
digest: the thesis, a page at a time
the library until the bells
a chapter drafted and torn up

label: Italian
blurb: The city's own language, and the lectures are in it. Forty hours to follow a sermon; a lifetime to argue in one.

credentialAfter.line: You dream in Italian now, badly. The Romans have stopped switching to English for you.

digest: Italian with the Sisters
the subjunctive, in Italian this time
a newspaper read with a dictionary

label: The chapel
blurb: The college chapel before the city wakes. Rome is loud; this is not.
digest: the chapel at six
an hour before the tabernacle, with the traffic outside
the holy hour nobody saw

label: Hospital chaplaincy
blurb: The Gemelli wants an English-speaking priest for the foreigners who die there. In Washington, Georgetown does.
digest: the hospital wards
a death in a language you barely have
the night pager, again

label: Sunday supply at a parish
blurb: An English-speaking parish needs a priest for the noon Mass and the baptisms. The pastor pays in dinners.
digest: the noon Mass for the expatriates
a baptism in three languages
Sunday supply, and lunch after

label: Confessions at the basilica
blurb: The Penitentiary keeps a box for every language. Yours is English, until your Italian is good enough for the box next door.
digest: the box at St. Peter's
confessions for the pilgrims, in two languages
an afternoon in the basilica hearing the world

label: Confessions at the Shrine
blurb: The Basilica of the National Shrine keeps its confessionals busy, and a canon lawyer in training is still a priest.
digest: the confessionals at the Shrine
an afternoon of pilgrims' confessions

label: The college office
blurb: The rector needs someone who can run a calendar and a budget. It is not glamorous and the rector writes to bishops.
digest: the rector's calendar, kept
a budget reconciled for the college
letters to bishops, drafted for the rector

label: Work at the Holy See
blurb: A dicastery wants an American who can write a memo. It is the most watched desk a student can sit at, and the men who sit at it are remembered.

onFirst.key: sat at a desk in the Curia

digest: a memo for the dicastery
the Curia's corridors, which are longer than they look
an afternoon at the Holy See

label: The tribunal internship
blurb: The archdiocesan tribunal takes students for the case files. Every marriage in the city passes through in paper.
digest: case files at the tribunal
a defender of the bond's afternoon
the tribunal, and a marriage on paper

label: Guiding pilgrims
blurb: Groups from home want a priest who knows the city. You know the city. They tip in gratitude and in gossip.
digest: pilgrims from home, and the Scavi tour
a group from {diocese} at the Holy Door
guiding pilgrims, and hearing the news from home

label: The bishops' conference
blurb: The USCCB takes a student for the committee memos. You will meet every bishop's secretary in the country.
digest: committee memos at the conference
an afternoon on Fourth Street
the bishops' conference, and its secretaries

label: The Roman table
blurb: Dinner with the men who will be bishops, and the monsignori who decide which. The address book fills. So does the waistline.
digest: dinner with the future
a trattoria and an archbishop's secretary
the long table, and who was at it

label: Calcio and the walk
blurb: The college pitch on Saturdays, and the long walk back over the river. The body keeps its own accounts here too.
digest: calcio, lost to the Irish
the long walk home over the Tiber
a run before the heat

label: The bishop's calendar
blurb: Who sees him, when, and for how long. The most powerful ten minutes in the diocese are the ones you decide to give.
digest: the calendar, kept
a pastor who did not get his ten minutes
the week planned to the quarter hour

label: The car and the door
blurb: You drive him, you wait outside the door, and you know who was inside. He talks in the car, or does not.
digest: four hundred miles with the bishop
the door, and who came through it
the long drive back, and what he said

label: Master of ceremonies
blurb: Every pontifical Mass, every ordination, every funeral of a priest. The rubrics, the mitre, the crozier, and the man who hands them over.
digest: the mitre and the crozier, handed over
an ordination run to the minute
a priest's funeral, managed

label: The residence chapel
blurb: Mass for the sisters who cook, and an hour of your own in a chapel with nobody in it.
digest: Mass for the sisters
the chapel at the residence, alone
an hour before the tabernacle nobody else uses

label: The phone
blurb: Every priest of the diocese calls you to reach him. How you answer is what they think of you for thirty years.
digest: the phone, answered kindly
a pastor talked down before he reached the bishop
calls returned, all of them

label: Weekend supply
blurb: A parish somewhere needs Sunday Masses, and you are still a priest. It is the only pew you see.
digest: Sunday supply, somewhere in the diocese
three Masses in a parish that does not know you
a weekend in a pulpit

label: The Sunday night Mass
blurb: Ninety students and a guitar you cannot get rid of. The homily has to be able to take any question afterward.
digest: the Sunday night Mass, full
a homily argued with afterward
ninety students and the guitar

label: The discussion series
blurb: Hell, the priest before you, celibacy, the Crusades. Every question, and the ones who leave the Church leave from your chapel.
digest: the Thursday series, and a question about Hell
an argument that went past midnight
a student who came back

label: The open door
blurb: Office hours that are not office hours: the student who cannot sleep, the one who is leaving, the one who wants to be a priest.
digest: the door, open until one
a student who wants to be a priest
the one who is leaving, and the hour with him

label: The faculty table
blurb: Lunch with the professors who tolerate a priest. The town hears what you say there.
digest: lunch with the faculty
a philosophy professor who wants to argue
the faculty club, and its opinions

label: Sunday supply in town
blurb: A parish near the campus needs the noon Mass. It keeps you a parish priest.
digest: the noon Mass in town
Sunday supply, and a baptism

label: The wards
blurb: Room to room, the sick and the dying and the ones who will walk out. You learn to say nothing well.
digest: the wards, room by room
a death on the fourth floor
the oncology unit, and the woman who laughed

label: The night pager
blurb: Anointings at three in the morning. The families in the hallway remember who came.
digest: the pager at three
an anointing in the emergency room
the hallway, and the family who waited

label: The ethics committee
blurb: The physicians, the lawyer, and you, on the cases that have no good answer. The diocese's bioethics voice, whether you meant to be or not.
digest: the ethics committee, and a case with no answer
a physician who wanted the Church's view and got yours

label: The hospital chapel
blurb: Mass at noon for the staff who come, and an hour of your own after. The chapel is the one room in the building where nobody is dying.
digest: Mass for the nurses
the chapel between rounds

label: Weekend supply
blurb: A parish somewhere needs the Sunday Masses, and you are still a parish priest on Sundays.
digest: Sunday supply, and lunch after
three Masses in a parish that borrowed you

label: The Sunday Mass
blurb: A Sunday Mass in the chapel for the patients who can be wheeled down, the families who cannot leave, and the nurses between shifts. Communion carried to the floors after. The building learns it has a parish.
digest: the Sunday Mass in the chapel, and Communion to the floors
a wheelchair in every aisle at the ten o'clock
the chapel full, for once, and a nurse reading

label: The Spanish Mass
blurb: A Saturday evening Mass in Spanish for the families on the floors and the housekeeping staff who have never been asked. The word goes out through the kitchens.
digest: the Spanish Mass on Saturday, and the kitchens emptied for it
a rosary in Spanish on the sixth floor after

label: Confessions on the wards
blurb: Posted hours, a stole in your pocket, and a chair pulled to the bed. Half the floor has not been in twenty years, and a hospital bed is where they remember.
digest: confessions, bed to bed, on the posted hours
a man who had not been in forty years, and cried
the stole and the chair, on five

label: The unit and the emergency room
blurb: The two doors the pager sends you through most. The trauma bay at midnight, the intensive care unit at dawn, and the staff who learn your face there before they learn your name.
digest: the unit at dawn, and the trauma bay after
an anointing through the door of a helicopter
the ICU, where the staff know your coffee

label: Instruction at the bedside
blurb: The ones who ask: the lapsed, the never-baptized, the husband of forty years who came to Mass every Sunday and never joined. Catechesis in a chair, at their pace, which is not always slow enough.
digest: the Creed, a line at a time, on four
a man of eighty asking what happens at the Offertory
instruction at the bedside, and a profession of faith by Friday

label: Hospice
blurb: The hospital's hospice and the homes it sends people to. Slow deaths, long conversations, and families who have had time to decide what they think of priests.
digest: hospice, and a house with the furniture moved for the bed
a death that took all of Thursday, and was ready
the hospice nurse, who calls you first now

label: The volunteers
blurb: Eucharistic ministers from the parishes, trained, scheduled, and sent to the floors you cannot reach. A ministry grows by other hands, and the parishes remember whose idea it was.
digest: a Saturday training the volunteers
the volunteer schedule, and every floor covered on Sunday
forty names on the rota, and one who does not show

label: The chaplains' office
blurb: The budget line, the on-call rota, the meeting with the administrator, the paperwork the hospital wants and the diocese never reads. Somebody has to run it, and it decides whether there is a chaplaincy after you.
digest: the chaplaincy budget, argued line by line
the on-call rota, rewritten so somebody sleeps
a meeting with the administrator that was about metrics

label: The second chaplain
blurb: The diocese lends a deacon, or the hospital hires a lay chaplain, and you are the one who trains and covers. The pager rings less. The floors are seen more.
digest: the deacon's first night on the pager, and your phone by the bed anyway
the second chaplain, and a floor you had never had time for

label: The lectures
blurb: Two courses a semester to men who decided what they think of you from the way you walked in. Teach.
digest: dogmatics at nine, to twenty-two men
a lecture that landed
a question from the back row you could not answer

label: The formation reports
blurb: A dozen men a year, and a paragraph on each that goes to a bishop. What you write follows them.
digest: formation reports, twelve of them
a paragraph that will follow a man for years

label: Spiritual direction
blurb: Four seminarians an hour a week each, in the internal forum, where what is said stays.
digest: direction, four men, four hours
a directee who said the true thing

label: Sunday supply
blurb: The parishes near the seminary borrow the faculty on Sundays. It keeps you a parish priest.
digest: Sunday supply, borrowed by a parish
a wedding for a former student

label: Writing
blurb: The article the journal asked for, the book you keep not starting. Faculty are expected to publish.
digest: the article, revised again
a chapter drafted between lectures

label: The bishop's door
blurb: The hour before his day starts, when he asks what you think and sometimes means it. Everything else in the building runs on what is said here.
digest: twenty minutes with the bishop before his first appointment
the bishop asked what you would do, and you told him
a decision he will announce as his own, which it is now

label: The personnel board
blurb: Every assignment in the diocese crosses this table, and every priest knows whose hand moved him. Chair it well and the presbyterate trusts the process; chair it badly and they learn your name.
digest: the board, and a pastor who will not know until Friday why he is moving
two hours on one difficult parish and the four men who could take it
a vicar's letter read aloud at the table, and a silence after

label: The closings
blurb: The list of parishes the diocese cannot staff or afford, which the bishop will sign and you will have written. The towns will remember who wrote it.
digest: the closings list, revised, one name back on and one name off
a drive out to a parish that is on the list and does not know it
a spreadsheet that is really a map of where the diocese is dying

label: The tribunal
blurb: Marriage cases and the odd penal process, read for the bishop by the man who signs for him. Canon law kept sharp; secrets kept sharper.
digest: three marriage cases and one you will not forget
a penal process read twice, and signed once
an afternoon with the judicial vicar and the code open between you

label: The money
blurb: The finance council, the assessment, the priests' pension fund and what has been borrowed against it. Nobody else reads the whole ledger.
digest: the finance council, and a number nobody said aloud
the assessment letters, signed, and a pastor on the phone within the hour
the pension fund, and a question you asked the auditor twice

label: Deanery visits
blurb: A different deanery each month: the pastors' dinner, the complaints, the man who is drinking and the man who is drowning. The chancery's face, at their table.
digest: dinner with the northern deanery, and what the dean said in the parking lot
a pastor who needed the vicar general to say it was all right to ask for help
forty miles out and forty back for a meeting that mattered

label: The confirmation circuit
blurb: Forty parishes a year, a homily that must be new each time and is not, a dinner with the pastor after. The people meet the diocese as you.
digest: confirmations in a parish you had never seen, and a pastor who wanted to talk after
the same homily, a different gym
a sacristan who told you how the last auxiliary did it

label: The vicariate
blurb: A third of the diocese is yours to visit, hear, and report on. The pastors learn quickly whether you carry their complaints up or bury them.
digest: the vicariate's deans, and what they said when the recorder was off
a rectory visit that ran to midnight
a pastor's complaint carried up, and the bishop's face when he heard it

label: Standing in for the bishop
blurb: Where he cannot be, you are: the funeral, the fundraiser, the meeting with the mayor. The diocese learns whether you can be trusted with his voice.
digest: the mayor's breakfast, in the bishop's chair
a funeral he could not reach, and the family's thanks addressed to him
a decision announced in his name that you had made

label: The seminary board
blurb: The men in formation pass across the table twice a year. The rector wants a bishop who will back him; the men want one who will hear them.
digest: the seminary board, and one name the rector would not say aloud
a formation report read twice
an afternoon with the men who will be the presbyterate

label: The Spanish-speaking parishes
blurb: The bishop has given you the growing half of the diocese, which is also the half without money. Confirmations of three hundred at a time, and a quinceañera every Saturday.
digest: three hundred confirmations, a mariachi, and a pastor near tears
a parish hall that is also a legal clinic on Tuesdays
a family who asked you to bless a truck

label: The press and the town
blurb: The bishop does not like cameras and you are the one who is sent. Every sentence is the diocese's now.
digest: a television interview cut to eleven seconds
the editorial board, and a question about the bishop you did not answer
a quote in the paper that the chancellor called about

label: The cathedral and the circuit
blurb: The chair is in the cathedral and the diocese is in the car. Confirmations in every parish, the Chrism Mass, the ordinations if there are any. The people know their bishop by whether he comes.
digest: confirmations two hundred miles from the cathedral, and a potluck
the Chrism Mass, every priest of the diocese in one room
a mission church with eleven people and a stove

label: The priests
blurb: Forty-odd men, every one of whom you must know, move, and keep. The personnel board is yours now, and every assignment has your name on the letter.
digest: a priest in your study for an hour, and what he finally said
the assignment list, and the one man who will not understand it
a deanery dinner where nobody mentioned the letter

label: The closings and the mergers
blurb: Eighty parishes and forty priests: the arithmetic every bishop of this see has faced and most have put off. The towns will remember which ones you closed.
digest: the map on the study wall with the pins moved
a town hall that ran three hours
a merger decree signed, and a phone that rang until midnight

label: The money
blurb: The annual appeal, the insurer, the pension fund, the cathedral roof. Nobody else in the diocese reads the whole ledger and the finance council would rather you did not either.
digest: the appeal letter, signed forty thousand times by machine
the insurer's man, and the number he would not put in writing
the pension fund, and a question the auditor could not answer

label: Vocations and the seminary
blurb: Three men in formation at a seminary two states away, and a diocese that needs twenty. Every dinner with a college student is recruiting. The one you ordain will be the presbyterate for forty years.
digest: a Newman Center dinner, and one young man who stayed after
the seminary's report on your three
an ordination retreat where you were the only bishop and the only cook

label: Rome and the conference
blurb: The quinquennial report, the ad limina, the nunciature's questions, and the bishops' conference twice a year in a hotel. The see is small; the letters are not.
digest: the quinquennial report, three hundred pages nobody in Rome will read
the conference in a hotel ballroom, and a cardinal who knew your name
a letter from the nunciature answered the same day

label: Mass for the nuns
blurb: A monastery of nuns near the college has no priest of its own for the early Mass: in Rome, a house of Benedictine nuns across the river; in Washington, the Poor Clares a few streets from campus. They pay in breakfast and in prayers, and they mean the prayers.
digest: the six-thirty Mass for the sisters
Mass in the nuns' chapel, and breakfast through the grille
a homily for twelve nuns who have heard better

label: Vespers with the monks
blurb: In Rome the Benedictines at Sant'Anselmo sing Vespers on the Aventine at seven, in Latin, and anyone may sit in the back. In Washington the Dominicans at the House of Studies sing Compline. An hour that asks nothing of you but to be there.
digest: Vespers on the Aventine
the psalms in Latin with the monks
Compline with the friars, and the walk back in the dark

label: A hand at the friary
blurb: The Missionaries of Charity feed the city's poor at San Gregorio on the Caelian and never have enough hands; the Capuchins' door is the same. In Washington it is the sisters' house in Northeast and the Franciscan Monastery's kitchen. Potatoes, a mop, a line of men who want a priest more than the soup.
digest: the soup kitchen at San Gregorio
peeling potatoes with the sisters
the friary door, and the line outside it

label: French
blurb: The Gregorian teaches it too, and the French seminarians at the college will talk to you in it if you let them. Sixty hours to read the theology in it.

credentialAfter.line: You can preach in French now, to the Haitians and the Africans and the one Québécois family, and read the older theology in it.

digest: French with the Alsatians at table
the subjunctive, in French
a page of de Lubac in the original

label: German
blurb: Half the reading list is in it and the German college is across the river. Sixty hours to read a page without the dictionary.

credentialAfter.line: You can read Ratzinger in German now, and say Mass for the old families at Christmas.

digest: German cases, at the Germanicum
a page of Ratzinger in the original
German with the Bavarian at table

label: The tiers
blurb: Cell to cell on the tiers with a guard who stops caring after the first month. Most of them do not want you. The ones who do want you badly.
digest: the tiers, and a man who talked for forty minutes
a cell with a photograph taped up and nothing else
the tier where nobody looked up

label: Mass in the chapel
blurb: Sunday in a room with bolted-down benches and a choir of four that gets to eleven if you let them sing what they like.
digest: Mass on the bolted benches
a man who served the Mass who has served it before, somewhere

label: The box that is a grille
blurb: Confessions through a grille that is actually a grille. Some of them are lying and you will not always know which, and it does not matter as much as you would think.
digest: the grille, and a thing with no absolution in it, only the telling
a man who came back after eleven years

label: The warden's office
blurb: The warden and the deputy warden and the paperwork of getting a man to a chapel. You are a nuisance until you are useful, and then you are on speed dial.
digest: the warden, and a form that took three weeks
a lockdown, and what a chaplain can do during one

label: The last corridor
blurb: The men with no date and the men with one. Nobody else on the staff goes there for any reason but the count.
digest: the last corridor, and a man who wanted to talk about baseball
a date that was set, and then was not

label: The gate, on release days
blurb: Standing at the gate on a Tuesday morning with a bus ticket and a telephone number for a parish that will have him. Most of them do not use it. Some do.
digest: a man at the gate with a bag and a number
a parish that took him, and a pastor who telephoned to say so

label: The stations
blurb: Six churches, none with a resident priest, the farthest at the end of a road that is a river in April. You are the priest of all of them, on a rota, and the rota is you.
digest: the stations, and Mass in a church with a wood stove and eleven people
the far station, and the family who had waited since Christmas

label: The language
blurb: An hour a day with a grandmother who is patient and a dictionary that is not. You are a man with a laminated card until you are not.
digest: the grandmother, and a word you will not forget
the first confession you heard without the card

label: The road
blurb: Four hundred miles a week in a truck the diocese bought used. The road is the parish: you visit on the way to the next station, and you are late everywhere.
digest: the road, and a truck that started
a house on the way with a sick man in it

label: The backlog
blurb: Two years of baptisms, first communions and weddings that waited for a priest. Whole families in one afternoon.
digest: a Saturday of eleven baptisms in one church
a wedding of a couple with three children at the altar rail

label: The house
blurb: A rectory at night with a wood stove and a satellite telephone that costs the diocese four dollars a minute. Leaving the door unlocked is a policy.
digest: the house, and a knock at ten at night
a night nobody came, which happens

label: Letters home
blurb: The bishop wants a report a quarter and the parish you left wants to know you are alive. Both get the same letter with the paragraphs in a different order.
digest: a letter to the bishop that says what it is like
a letter from the parish you left with a photograph in it

label: Mass in the field
blurb: Mass on the hood of a vehicle, or in a plywood chapel, or in a tent, for whoever is not on duty. The choir is one sergeant and he is good.
digest: Mass on the hood of a truck at dawn
a chapel of plywood and eleven men who needed it

label: The flight line
blurb: Being where the men are: the flight line, the motor pool, the chow hall at two in the morning. A chaplain who stays in the chapel is a chaplain nobody talks to.
digest: the flight line, and a kid who asked whether God minded
the motor pool, and the sergeant who did not want to talk and did

label: The command tent
blurb: The colonel and the sergeant major and the things a chaplain is allowed to say to them that nobody else is. You are the only man on the base with no rank that matters.
digest: the command tent, and a thing said to the colonel that needed saying
a briefing you were not supposed to be in

label: The sergeants
blurb: The men who actually run the unit, and who decide whether the chaplain is somebody or nobody. It takes a month and one specific thing.
digest: a sergeant who decided you were somebody
the sergeants' table, and a seat at it

label: When it goes wrong
blurb: The days that are not most days: the aid station, the flight out, the things that have to be said to nineteen-year-olds who were with him an hour ago.
digest: a day that was not most days
the aid station, and what was said there

label: Letters home
blurb: The men who cannot write the letter, and the letter that has to be written when the man cannot. You write a great many of both.
digest: four letters written for men who asked
a letter that took all night and was two paragraphs

label: The hours of direction
blurb: Twenty men, an hour each a month, in a room where nothing said leaves. The whole apparatus of the priesthood of the next forty years, an hour at a time.
digest: the hours, and a man who said the true thing in the fortieth minute
an hour in which nothing was said, and it was the right hour

label: The house chapel
blurb: The morning Office and the evening, in choir, with the men. A director who is not in the chapel is a man who is not seen praying.
digest: the chapel, and the house singing badly and well
an hour of adoration with four men and then eleven

label: The corridor
blurb: Being in the corridor when a man needs to find you. The door open, the light on, and the difference between a director on a list and one the house actually uses.
digest: the corridor at ten at night, and the knock
a man who walked past three times before he came in

label: The rector's counsel
blurb: The rector cannot ask what is said in direction and does not. What he can ask is whether the house is well, and you are the only man who can answer without breaking anything.
digest: the rector, and a question you could answer
the rector's office, and a man neither of you named

label: The house retreats
blurb: Preaching the house retreat, and the retreats of the classes, and the day of recollection in Advent. The men judge a director by his conferences before they judge him by anything else.
digest: a conference that landed
a retreat, and the silence that followed it

label: The one who knocks at midnight
blurb: The man in crisis: the fire escape in February, the one who is leaving, the one who should. Nothing you do this week is more important and nobody will ever know you did it.
digest: a knock at midnight, and a man who stayed
a man who left, and did it well, because somebody let him

label: The principals
blurb: Eleven principals, twice a year each, and the telephone every day. Some of them are running schools; some of them are running out of time.
digest: the principals' meeting, and the one who did not come
a principal who is very good and is leaving

label: The board
blurb: A board of donors and lawyers and one pastor who thinks the schools cost too much, and you, with the numbers.
digest: the board, and a vote that went the right way by one
a donor who wanted a wing named and got one

label: The enrolment
blurb: The marketing, the tuition assistance, the open houses, the kindergarten numbers that decide everything six years out.
digest: an open house with forty families
the kindergarten numbers, which were up

label: The school that cannot be saved
blurb: There is always one. The meeting in its gym, the parents, the pastor who blames you, and the letter that goes out in March.
digest: a gym full of parents, and the number said out loud
a school closed properly, which is still a school closed

label: What the teachers are paid
blurb: Eleven thousand less than the public district. The campaign, the foundation, the pastor who will not raise the subsidy, and the third-grade teacher who is being courted.
digest: a teacher kept, by four thousand dollars and a conversation
the foundation, and a cheque that was not enough

label: The classrooms
blurb: A morning a week in an actual school, with actual children, which a superintendent who does not do it stops understanding within a year.
digest: a second-grade classroom and a question about heaven
a school Mass with four hundred children and one acolyte who dropped the book
